text: Jacob Abraham Camille Pissarro (/pɪˈsɑːroʊ/ piss-AR-oh; French: [kamij pisaʁo]; 10 July 1830 – 13 November 1903) was a Danish-French Impressionist and Neo-Impressionist painter born on the island of St. Thomas (now in the US Virgin Islands, but then in the Danish West Indies). His significance lies in his contributions to both Impressionism and Post-Impressionism. Pissarro studied under major forerunners such as Gustave Courbet and Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot, and later worked with Georges Seurat and Paul Signac when he adopted the Neo-Impressionist style at the age of 54. Born on 10 July 1830 to Frederick Abraham Gabriel Pissarro and Rachel Manzano-Pomié, his father was of Portuguese Jewish descent and held French nationality, while his mother was from a French-Jewish family with Provençal Jewish roots. His father, a merchant who came to St. Thomas from France to manage the hardware store of his deceased uncle Isaac Petit, married his widow, which caused a stir in the island’s small Jewish community due to Jewish law prohibiting marriage between a man and his aunt. As a result, Pissarro’s four children were barred from attending the local Jewish school and were instead sent to an all-black primary school. Upon his death, his will divided his estate equally between the synagogue and St. Thomas’ Protestant church. At age twelve, Pissarro was sent to boarding school in France, attending the Savary Academy in Passy near Paris, where he developed an early appreciation for French art masters and was taught drawing and painting by Monsieur Savary, who encouraged him to draw from nature upon returning to St. Thomas. After returning to St. Thomas at age sixteen or seventeen, he worked as a port clerk in his father’s business, using every opportunity during the next five years to practice drawing. Visual theorist Nicholas Mirzoeff argues that the young Pissarro was inspired by the works of James Gay Sawkins, a British painter and geologist who lived in Charlotte Amalie, St. Thomas circa 1847, possibly attending art classes taught by Sawkins and viewing his paintings of Mitla, Mexico. Mirzoeff notes that Pissarro began drawing the local African population in imitation of Sawkins, creating sketches for a postslavery imagination. At age twenty-one, Danish artist Fritz Melbye inspired him to pursue painting as a full-time profession, becoming his teacher and friend. Pissarro then left his family and job to live in Venezuela, where he and Melbye spent two years working as artists in Caracas and La Guaira, drawing landscapes, village scenes, and numerous sketches that filled multiple sketchbooks. In 1855, at age 25, Pissarro moved to Paris and began working as an assistant to Anton Melbye, Fritz Melbye’s brother. He also studied the works of Courbet, Charles-François Daubigny, Jean-François Millet, and Corot, and enrolled in classes at institutions such as the École des Beaux-Arts and Académie Suisse, though he later found their teaching methods "stifling" and sought alternative instruction from Corot. His early paintings followed the standards required for display at the Paris Salon, the official body that dictated acceptable art. In 1859, his first painting was accepted and exhibited, and his subsequent works were influenced by Corot, who taught him to paint outdoors, or "plein air." Pissarro admired Corot and Courbet for their "statements of pictorial truth" and also appreciated Millet’s "sentimental renditions of rural life." During this period, he came to value expressing the beauties of nature without adulteration. After a year in Paris, he began painting in the countryside to capture the daily reality of village life, which he found "picturesque" and worthy of artistic representation—described as the "golden age of the peasantry." He later explained to a student that Corot completed his paintings in the studio and revised them, while Pissarro preferred to finish his works outdoors, often in one sitting, which gave his art a more realistic feel. This approach was sometimes criticized as "vulgar," with critics noting his depictions of "rutted and edged hodgepodge of bushes, mounds of earth, and trees in various stages of development," likened to modern art showing garbage cans or beer bottles on a street. This difference in style led to disagreements between Pissarro and Corot. In 1859, while attending the Académie Suisse, Pissarro became friends with younger artists including Claude Monet, Armand Guillaumin, and Paul Cézanne, all of whom shared dissatisfaction with the Salon. Cézanne’s work was mocked at the time, and in later years, Cézanne never forgot the sympathy and understanding Pissarro showed him. Pissarro supported the group’s belief in portraying individuals in natural settings without artifice or grandeur. In 1863, nearly all of their paintings were rejected by the Salon, and Emperor Napoleon III placed them in a separate exhibit, the Salon des Refusés, where only Pissarro and Cézanne’s works were included, provoking hostility from the Salon officials and the public. In 1864, Pissarro was accepted into the official Salon for the first time, and in 1865 and 1866, he credited Melbye and Corot as influences in the exhibition catalog. By 1868, he no longer credited other artists, effectively declaring his independence as a painter—a shift noted by art critic Émile Zola. At age thirty-eight, Pissarro had earned a reputation as a landscapist rivaling Corot and Daubigny. In the late 1860s or early 1870s, Pissarro became fascinated with Japanese prints, which influenced his desire to experiment with new compositions. He described this interest to his son Lucien. In 1871, in Croydon, England, he married Julie Vellay (1838–1926), a vineyard grower’s daughter and his mother’s maid, with whom he had seven children, six of whom became painters: Lucien Pissarro (1863–1944), Georges Henri Manzana Pissarro (1871–1961), Félix Pissarro (1874–1897), Ludovic-Rodo Pissarro (1878–1952), Jeanne Bonin-Pissarro (1881–1948), and Paul-Émile Pissarro (1884–1972). The family lived outside Paris in Pontoise and later in Louveciennes, both of which inspired many of his paintings, including scenes of village life, rivers, woods, and people at work. He maintained contact with earlier artists such as Monet, Renoir, Cézanne, and Frédéric Bazille. Pissarro was involved in anarchist circles and held strong egalitarian views, subscribing to the radical anarchist publication Le Révolté and communicating with leading theorist Jean Grave and fellow anarchist artists Paul Signac and Henri-Edmond Cross. His political beliefs influenced his art; in 1889, he created an album of 30 drawings titled Turpitudes sociales, using caricature and allegory to critique modern societal issues, intended as a gift for his niece to reinforce her anarchist views. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–71, having only Danish nationality and unable to join the army, he moved his family to Norwood, a village on the edge of London. His style, a forerunner of Impressionism, did not gain acceptance, and he wrote to his friend Théodore Duret that "my painting doesn't catch on, not at all." He met Paris art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel in London, who became his primary dealer for most of his life and introduced him to Monet, who was also in London. They both studied the works of British landscape artists John Constable and J. M. W. Turner, which reinforced their belief that open-air painting provided the truest depiction of light and atmosphere, an effect unattainable in the studio. Pissarro’s paintings began to feature more spontaneous brushwork and impasto, adding depth. During his time in England, he recorded Sydenham and the Norwoods, just after they were connected by railways and before suburban expansion. One of the largest paintings from this period is a view of St. Bartholomew’s Church at Lawrie Park Avenue, known as The Avenue, Sydenham, now in the National Gallery in London. Twelve oil paintings from his stay in Upper Norwood are listed in a 1939 catalogue raisonné prepared by his fifth child Ludovic-Rodolphe Pissarro and Lionello Venturi, including Lower Norwood Under Snow, Lordship Lane Station, views of The Crystal Palace relocated from Hyde Park, Dulwich College, Sydenham Hill, All Saints Church Upper Norwood, and a lost painting of St. Stephen’s Church. Returning to France, Pissarro lived in Pontoise from 1872 to 1884. In 1890, he visited England again and painted ten scenes of central London. He returned in 1892 to paint in Kew Gardens and Kew Green, and in 1897, produced several oils described as being of Bedford Park and Chiswick, though all were actually of the nearby Stamford Brook area except one of Bath Road, which runs from Stamford Brook along the south edge of Bedford Park. Upon returning to France after the war, he discovered that of the 1,500 paintings he had created over 20 years, which he had left behind in London, only 40 remained; the rest were damaged or destroyed by soldiers who used them as floor mats in the mud. It is assumed many of the lost works were in the Impressionist style he was developing, thereby "documenting the birth of Impressionism." Critic Armand Silvestre called Pissarro "basically the inventor of this [Impressionist] painting," though his role was described as "less that of the great man of ideas than that of the good counselor and appeaser," with Monet seen as the guiding force. Pissarro soon reestablished friendships with earlier Impressionist artists such as Cézanne, Monet, Manet, Renoir, and Degas, and expressed a desire for an alternative to the Salon to showcase their unique styles. In 1873, he helped establish a collective called the "Société Anonyme des Artistes, Peintres, Sculpteurs et Graveurs," which included fifteen artists. Pissarro created the group’s first charter and became the "pivotal" figure in establishing and maintaining the group. With his prematurely grey beard, the forty-three-year-old Pissarro was regarded as a "wise elder and father figure" by the group, though he worked on equal terms with others due to his youthful temperament and creativity. The following year, in 1874, the group held their First Impressionist Exhibition, which shocked and "horrified" critics who valued only religious, historical, or mythological subjects. Critics found fault with the Impressionist works on multiple grounds. Pissarro exhibited five landscapes at the exhibit, and Émile Zola praised his art. In 1876, art critic Albert Wolff complained that "trees are not violet, that sky is not the color of fresh butter," while journalist and critic Octave Mirbeau noted that "Camille Pissarro has been a revolutionary through the revitalized working methods with which he has endowed painting." According to art historian John Rewald, Pissarro adopted a simpler, more natural attitude than the other artists. In later years, Cézanne referred to Pissarro as "the first Impressionist." In 1906, a few years after Pissarro’s death, Cézanne, then 67 and a role model for new artists, paid Pissarro a debt of gratitude by listing himself in an exhibition catalogue as "Paul Cézanne, pupil of Pissarro." Pissarro, Degas, and American impressionist Mary Cassatt planned a journal of their original prints in the late 1870s, a project that failed when Degas withdrew. Art historian and the artist’s great-grandson Joachim Pissarro notes that they "professed a passionate disdain for the Salons and refused to exhibit at them," sharing an "almost militant resolution" against the Salon, with their mutual admiration rooted in a kinship of ethical values.

Camille Pissarro was recognized by Cézanne as "the first Impressionist," and in 1906, at age 67, Cézanne listed himself in an exhibition catalogue as "Paul Cézanne, pupil of Pissarro" as a gesture of gratitude. In the late 1870s, Pissarro, Degas, and American impressionist Mary Cassatt planned a journal of their original prints, but the project failed when Degas withdrew. All three artists expressed a passionate disdain for the Paris Salon and refused to exhibit there, sharing an "almost militant resolution" against it, with mutual admiration rooted in both aesthetic and ethical concerns. Cassatt, who joined Pissarro’s French Impressionist group and gave up U.S. exhibition opportunities, was often treated as an outsider by the Salon due to her non-French nationality and lack of citizenship, but she was deeply committed to promoting Impressionism and exhibited out of solidarity with her friends. By the end of the 1890s, she distanced herself from Degas, whose sharp tongue she found difficult to defend against, and preferred the company of Pissarro, whom she described as a teacher "that could have taught the stones to draw correctly." Pissarro experimented with lithographs, woodblock engravings, and multicolor etching and monotype, and art historian Cora Michael noted he was the most devoted Impressionist to printmaking, approaching prints as an avant-garde artist. From the 1880s to the early 1890s, he returned to his studio in Pontoise, producing works such as "Vegetable Market at Pontoise" and "The Road to Rouen: The Hills of Pontoise" using various print mediums. In the 1880s, Pissarro began exploring new themes and methods to escape what he saw as an artistic "mire," returning to depictions of rural life and peasants, a theme he had previously explored in Venezuela, with Degas describing these subjects as "peasants working to make a living." This period marked the end of the Impressionist movement, as Joachim Pissarro noted: "Once such a die-hard Impressionist as Pissarro had turned his back on Impressionism, it was apparent that Impressionism had no chance of surviving." Pissarro intended to "educate the public" by painting people at work or at home in realistic, non-idealized settings, a style praised by Renoir in 1882 as "revolutionary" for portraying the "common man." Though he did not overtly preach political messages, his choice of humble subjects was intended to appeal to his upper-class clientele. He also adopted a more unified brushwork and pure color strokes. In 1885, Pissarro met Georges Seurat and Paul Signac, who used a scientific theory of painting involving small patches of pure color to create blended effects; Pissarro practiced this pointillist technique from 1885 to 1888, with his works displayed in the 1886 Impressionist Exhibition under a separate section alongside Seurat, Signac, and his son Lucien. All four works were considered an "exception" to the eighth exhibition, and Joachim Pissarro notes that every reviewer acknowledged Pissarro’s "extraordinary capacity to change his art, revise his position and take on new challenges." Pissarro described the new style as a "phase in the logical march of Impressionism," making him the only Impressionist to hold this view, and thus the only artist to transition from Impressionism to Neo-Impressionism. In 1884, art dealer Theo van Gogh asked Pissarro to take his brother Vincent as a boarder, and although Vincent never stayed, Pissarro was impressed by his work and explained to him how to find and express light and color, ideas Vincent later used in his paintings. Pissarro eventually rejected Neo-Impressionism, calling its system too artificial, and after returning to his earlier style, his work became, according to Rewald, "more subtle, his color scheme more refined, his drawing firmer," reflecting increased mastery in old age. However, this artistic evolution contributed to his ongoing financial hardship, which persisted until his 60s. Joachim Pissarro attributes this to Pissarro’s "lack of fear of the immediate repercussions" of his stylistic choices and notes that his work provided strength to sustain his morale. His contemporaries viewed his independence as a "mark of integrity" and referred to him as "Père Pissarro" (father Pissarro). In later years, Pissarro suffered from a recurring eye infection that limited outdoor work to warm weather, leading him to paint from hotel rooms in Rouen, Paris, Le Havre, Dieppe, and London, often choosing upper floors for broader views. He died in Paris on 13 November 1903 and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery. Art critic Armand Silvestre called Pissarro the "most real and most naive member" of the Impressionists, and art historian Diane Kelder described his work as expressing "the same quiet dignity, sincerity, and durability that distinguished his person," noting he mediated internal disputes within the group and was a diligent proselytizer of the new painting. Lucien Pissarro, Pissarro’s son, recalls that Pissarro painted regularly with Cézanne beginning in 1872, with Cézanne walking several miles to join him in Pontoise. Cézanne admired Pissarro’s 1860s landscapes and referred to him as a "father for me," a "man to consult and a little like the good Lord." Lucien was taught painting by his father and described him as a "splendid teacher, never imposing his personality on his pupil." Gauguin, who studied under Pissarro, referred to him as a "force with which future artists would have to reckon," and Pissarro introduced Gauguin to Degas and Cézanne. In a 1902 letter near the end of his life, Gauguin wrote of Pissarro’s influence. Mary Cassatt, who lived in Paris to study art and joined the Impressionist group, also noted that Pissarro was "such a teacher that he could have taught the stones to draw correctly." Caribbean author Derek Walcott based his 2000 book-length poem, *Tiepolo's Hound*, on Pissarro’s life. Pissarro is a central character in R.w. Meek’s historical fiction novels, *The Dream Collector*, Books I & II, depicting his role among the Impressionists and his openness to the Post-Impressionist works of Seurat, Gauguin, and van Gogh. During the early 1930s, Jewish art collectors in Europe were forced to sell or give up their collections due to Nazi anti-Jewish laws, with artworks looted by organizations like the Reichsleiter Rosenberg Taskforce. Several Pissarro paintings were looted: "Shepherdess Bringing Home the Sheep" was taken from Yvonne et Raoul Meyer in France in 1941, passed through Switzerland and New York, and entered the Fred Jones Jr Museum at the University of Oklahoma; in 2014, Meyer’s daughter Léonie-Noëlle filed a restitution claim, resulting in a five-year transfer to France with a three-year rotation between Paris and Oklahoma, though in 2020 she challenged the agreement and later abandoned the effort after the museum sued for financial penalties. "Picking Peas" was looted from Jewish businessman Simon Bauer in 1943, along with 92 other artworks seized by the Vichy regime. "Sower And Ploughman" was owned by Dr. Henri Hinrichsen of Leipzig until 11 January 1940, when he was forced to surrender it to Hildebrand Gurlitt in Nazi-occupied Brussels before being murdered in Auschwitz in September 1942. "Le Quai Malaquais, Printemps" passed through the hands of Nazi art looter Bruno Lohse after being owned by German Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer. "Le Boulevard de Montmartre, Matinée de Printemps," owned by Max Silberberg, a German Jewish industrialist whose collection was considered one of the best in pre-war Germany, was seized and sold in a forced auction before Silberberg and his wife were murdered in Auschwitz. After WWII, many artworks were found in European and American museums with false provenances; some were returned to original owners through legal action, and many were later donated to museums. One such piece, the 1897 oil painting *Rue St. Honoré, Apres Midi, Effet de Pluie*, was discovered in Madrid’s Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza in 2011, and the Spanish government denied a U.S. request to return it; a Los Angeles court ruled in favor of the Thyssen-Bornemisza Foundation, and in November 2025, California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta announced state intervention. In 1999, *Le Boulevard de Montmartre, Matinée de Printemps* appeared at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem with an unaware donor; in January 2012, *Le Marché aux Poissons* (The Fish Market), a color monotype, was returned after 30 years. During his lifetime, Pissarro sold few paintings, but by the 21st century, his works were selling for millions. On 6 November 2007, Christie’s in New York sold four paintings, *Les Quatre Saisons*, for $14,601,000 (estimate $12,000,000 – $18,000,000). In November 2009, *Le Pont Boieldieu et la Gare d'Orléans, Rouen, Soleil* sold for $7,026,500 at Sotheby’s in New York. In February 2014, *Le Boulevard de Montmartre, Matinée de Printemps*, originally owned by Max Silberberg, sold at Sotheby’s in London for £19.9M, nearly five times the previous record. In October 2021, Berlin’s Alte Nationalgalerie restituted *A Square in La Roche-Guyon* (1867) to the heirs of Armand Dorville, a French Jewish art collector whose family was persecuted by the Nazis and whose paintings were sold at a 1942 auction in Nice overseen by the Commissariat Général aux Questions Juives; the museum then repurchased the painting. Camille’s son Lucien, and his second and third sons Georges Henri Manzana Pissarro and Félix Pissarro, were Impressionist and Neo-impressionist painters; Lucien’s daughter Orovida Pissarro was also a painter. Camille’s great-grandson Joachim Pissarro became Head Curator of Drawing and Painting at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City and a professor at Hunter College’s Art Department. Camille’s great-granddaughter Lélia Pissarro has had her work exhibited alongside her great-grandfather, and Julia Pissarro, a Barnard College graduate, is active in the art scene. From Camille’s only daughter, Jeanne Pissarro, other painters include Henri Bonin-Pissarro (1918–2003) and Claude Bonin-Pissarro (born 1921), father of Abstract artist Frédéric Bonin-Pissarro (born 1964). Hugues Claude Pissarro (dit Pomié), Camille’s grandson, born in 1935 in Neuilly-sur-Seine, began drawing and painting as a child under his father’s guidance, studied the great masters at the Louvre, and was commissioned by the White House in 1959 to paint a portrait of President Dwight Eisenhower; he now lives and paints in Donegal, Ireland, with his wife Corinne and their children. The Stern Pissarro Gallery in London specializes in works by the family and provides research and authentication services for artworks attributed to several of Camille Pissarro’s descendants.

During his adolescence and early twenties, he studied the works of the great masters at the Louvre. His artwork has been showcased in exhibitions across Europe and the United States, and in 1959, he was commissioned by the White House to paint a portrait of U.S. President Dwight Eisenhower. He currently resides in Donegal, Ireland, where he paints alongside his wife Corinne, who is also an accomplished artist, and their children. The Stern Pissarro Gallery in London focuses on works by the Pissarro family and offers a research and authentication service for artworks attributed to several of Camille Pissarro's descendants.
